## Technology Stack Analysis

### Obsidian Core Platform

Obsidian is a local-first, Markdown-based knowledge management tool with an extensible plugin architecture. It stores all data as plain `.md` files on disk, making it fully interoperable with any tool that reads Markdown. As of 2025-2026, Obsidian has matured into a comprehensive PKM (Personal Knowledge Management) platform used at scale — one practitioner documented 8,000 notes with 64,000+ internal links managed over 3+ years.

_Core Architecture: Local-first markdown files, YAML frontmatter metadata, wiki-link graph, plugin extensibility_
_Current Version: 1.9+ with Properties system, Canvas, and Bases (database views)_
_Strengths: Zero vendor lock-in, offline-first, plain-text portability, massive plugin ecosystem_
_Source: [Obsidian Help](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [PKM at Scale](https://www.dsebastien.net/personal-knowledge-management-at-scale-analyzing-8-000-notes-and-64-000-links/)_

### Properties & Metadata System (YAML Frontmatter)

Obsidian supports 7 property types: **Text**, **List**, **Number**, **Checkbox**, **Date**, **Date & Time**, and **Tags**. Properties are stored as YAML frontmatter and enforced vault-wide — once a property name is assigned a type, ALL notes with that property must use the same type.

_Supported Types: text, list, number, checkbox, date, datetime, tags_
_Default Properties: `tags` (hierarchical), `aliases` (search), `cssclasses` (styling)_
_Limitation: No nested YAML support in visual editor (Source mode only for complex structures)_
_Vault-Wide Enforcement: Property type is consistent across entire vault_
_Source: [Obsidian Properties](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [DeepWiki Properties](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-help/4.3-properties-and-metadata)_

### Canvas System (JSON-Based Visual Workspace)

Canvas files (`.canvas`) use an open JSON format ([JSON Canvas spec](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)) with 4 node types: **file** (vault references), **text** (markdown), **link** (URLs), and **group** (containers). Edges connect nodes with directional arrows. Since canvas files are plain JSON, they can be programmatically generated, manipulated, and queried.

_Node Types: file, text, link, group — each with x/y/width/height positioning_
_Edge System: fromNode/toNode with side anchoring (top/right/bottom/left) and labels_
_Color System: 6 palette presets or hex values_
_Programmatic Tools: canvas_lib.py, obsidian-node-canvas, Advanced Canvas plugin_
_Source: [Canvas Help](https://help.obsidian.md/plugins/canvas), [Canvas API DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/4.1-canvas-api), [JSON Canvas GitHub](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)_

### Dataview Plugin (Query Engine)

Dataview treats an Obsidian vault as a queryable database. It indexes YAML frontmatter and inline fields (`[key:: value]`) and provides both a DQL query language and a JavaScript API (DataviewJS). It now uses IndexedDB caching for near-instant startup on repeat visits.

_Query Modes: DQL (table/list/task/calendar) and DataviewJS (full JavaScript)_
_Data Sources: YAML frontmatter, inline fields `[key:: value]`, tags, tasks_
_Caching: IndexedDB for fast startup on large vaults_
_Limitation: Read-only by design — cannot modify notes, only display/query_
_Source: [Dataview GitHub](https://github.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview), [Dataview Docs](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/), [Dataview API](https://deepwiki.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview/4-api-reference)_

### Templater Plugin (Template Automation)

Templater (3.8M+ downloads, 4,616 GitHub stars) provides dynamic template insertion with JavaScript execution. It supports conditional logic, file manipulation, system commands, and user prompt inputs. Combined with Dataview, it transforms Obsidian into an automation platform.

_Template Syntax: `<% %>` (variable expansion), `<%* %>` (JavaScript execution)_
_Capabilities: File creation, folder manipulation, date math, system commands, user prompts_
_Automation: Auto-apply templates on note creation, folder-based template matching_
_Source: [Templater GitHub](https://github.com/SilentVoid13/Templater), [Templater Scripts](https://github.com/mihaiconstantin/obsidian-templater-scripts)_

### Obsidian MCP Server Ecosystem (6+ Projects)

The MCP ecosystem for Obsidian has exploded in 2025-2026 with at least 24 MCP servers listed on mcp.so. Key implementations:

| Server | Approach | Key Differentiator |
|--------|----------|--------------------|
| [cyanheads/obsidian-mcp-server](https://github.com/cyanheads/obsidian-mcp-server) | REST API bridge | Comprehensive CRUD + frontmatter + tags |
| [bitbonsai/mcp-obsidian](https://github.com/bitbonsai/mcp-obsidian) | Universal AI bridge | Multi-client (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) + YAML safety |
| [aaronsb/obsidian-mcp-plugin](https://github.com/aaronsb/obsidian-mcp-plugin) | Graph-first | Semantic navigation + knowledge graph traversal |
| [jacksteamdev/obsidian-mcp-tools](https://github.com/jacksteamdev/obsidian-mcp-tools) | Semantic search | Vector search + Templater integration |
| [fiddeb/obsidian-mcp-server](https://lobehub.com/mcp/fiddeb-obsidian-mcp-server) | Go-based | Lightweight, VS Code integration |

_Ecosystem Size: 24+ MCP servers for Obsidian on mcp.so_
_Common Pattern: Obsidian Local REST API plugin as backend bridge_
_Source: [Obsidian Forum Discussion](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/obsidian-mcp-servers-experiences-and-recommendations/99936)_

### Cohezion Vault MCP Server (Current State)

Our existing server (`cloud-vault-mcp/`) implements **47 tools** across 12 categories in ~10,475 lines of Python. It runs as a FastMCP HTTP server on port 8360.

| Category | Tools | Purpose |
|----------|-------|---------|
| Core Vault Ops | 5 | Read/write/edit/delete/list notes |
| Obsidian-Aware | 4 | Backlinks, forward links, tags, templates |
| Full-Text Search | 1 | Regex search with folder scoping |
| Compound Engineering | 5 | Decisions, experiments, patterns, context search |
| Teleport Protocol | 5 | Cross-session task delegation |
| Session Context | 3 | State push/pull, memory bridge |
| Google Sheets | 6 | Research spreadsheet bridge |
| SurrealDB Graph | 5 | Graph sync, watchers, queries |
| Ollama Integration | 3 | Local LLM queries + embeddings |
| Agent Context | 3 | Session tracking, decision/outcome lineage |
| Text-to-Speech | 1 | Pocket TTS |
| Health Check | 1 | Full dependency health check |

_Templates: 6 types (decisions, experiments, patterns, papers, daily, projects)_
_Frontmatter: Standard YAML with date, tags, status, project fields_
_Security: Path validation, traversal prevention, optional TLS + API key auth_
_**GAP: No BMAD workflow integration (PRD, Architecture, Epics, Stories)**_

### Technology Adoption Trends

_MCP as Standard: Anthropic's MCP protocol has become the de facto AI-tool integration standard, with 24+ Obsidian implementations alone_
_Graph-First Knowledge: The trend is moving from flat file search toward semantic graph navigation (aaronsb's approach)_
_AI-Native Workflows: Users report 8-12 hours/week saved via AI-assisted Obsidian documentation workflows_
_Schema.org Integration: Emerging pattern of YAML-LD frontmatter for linked data compatibility_
_Source: [Obsidian AI Review](https://tutorialswithai.com/tools/obsidian-ai/), [Full Stack CX Workflow](https://www.fullstack.cx/blog/obsidian-documentation-workflow), [Schema.org Forum](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/schema-org-in-obsidian-using-yaml-ld-frontmatter-for-linked-data/109969)_

Here's a summary of the findings on Obsidian vault scalability, architecture, and large vault performance:

## Obsidian Vault Scalability & Large Vault Performance

### Core Architecture

Obsidian is a web application hosted in a local web browser environment called Electron, operating on a folder of files stored locally on your computer, which it calls the Vault. The expectation is that Obsidian should be very scalable because it stores documents and attachments in the computer's file system — all it needs to maintain is an index database to aid full-text search and the maintenance/navigation of links.

### Large Vault Challenges

**Indexing at Scale:**
- A 130K-note open-source vault (nixpkgs-vault) takes around 10 minutes to index, even on a powerful computer with an Intel i7-14700KF, 64 GB RAM, and NVIDIA 4090.
- Users have reported that the app fails to complete indexing when there are a large number of files — e.g., a vault with over 113K files had issues completing the indexing process.

**Mobile Performance:**
- Vaults with over 50K notes + 40K attachments on Android can have a ~3 minute vault load time and ~27 minute reindexing time, with reindexing happening on every vault load.

**Graph View:**
- Even without third-party plugins, the graph view struggles at extreme scales — one user wanted to visualize a 130K-note vault and found the graph view didn't work properly.

**Link Autocomplete:**
- The notes selector (when typing between `[[ ]]`) can be very slow for large vaults, taking up to 4 seconds between each letter typed.

### Massive Vault Use Cases

Some users aim to grow Obsidian-managed data at ~1TB/year (99% non-text autogenerated data), using an "immutable data / store everything" approach with Obsidian as an indexing front end.

**Published Vaults:**
- Users maintaining large published vaults (e.g., 10K pages, 200 MB, 99.9% text) report slow first load times and problems with Google indexing.

### Modern Solutions (2025)

**MCP Server with SQLite Indexing:**
- The `obsidian-mcp` project features a complete architecture overhaul with 5x faster searches using persistent SQLite indexing, 90% less memory usage via efficient streaming architecture, regex power search, and incremental indexing (only re-indexes changed files).
- With persistent indexing, only changed files are re-indexed; concurrent operations use async I/O, making large vaults (10,000+ notes) usable.

**RAG Integration for Semantic Search:**
- Obsidian's plugin ecosystem in 2025 has evolved to support advanced integration with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, enabling AI-driven querying and synthesis workflows.
- For vector storage, 2025 benchmarks highlight Milvus, Pinecone, and Qdrant — Milvus with its cloud-native architecture supports HNSW, IVF, and DiskANN indexing and can handle billions of vectors with low-latency queries.

## Obsidian Vault Scalability & Large Vault Performance

### Core Architecture

Obsidian is a web application hosted in a local web browser environment called Electron, operating on a folder of files stored locally on your computer, which it calls the Vault. - Users have reported that the app fails to complete indexing when there are a large number of files — e.g., a vault with over 113K files had issues completing the indexing process.

**Mobile Performance:**
- Vaults with over 50K notes + 40K attachments on Android can have a ~3 minute vault load time and ~27 minute reindexing time, with reindexing happening on every vault load.

**Graph View:**
- Even without third-party plugins, the graph view struggles at extreme scales — one user wanted to visualize a 130K-note vault and found the graph view didn't work properly.

**Link Autocomplete:**
- The notes selector (when typing between `[[ ]]`) can be very slow for large vaults, taking up to 4 seconds between each letter typed.

### Massive Vault Use Cases

Some users aim to grow Obsidian-managed data at ~1TB/year (99% non-text autogenerated data), using an "immutable data / store everything" approach with Obsidian as an indexing front end.

**Published Vaults:**
- Users maintaining large published vaults (e.g., 10K pages, 200 MB, 99.9% text) report slow first load times and problems with Google indexing.

### Modern Solutions (2025)

**MCP Server with SQLite Indexing:**
- The `obsidian-mcp` project features a complete architecture overhaul with 5x faster searches using persistent SQLite indexing, 90% less memory usage via efficient streaming architecture, regex power search, and incremental indexing (only re-indexes changed files).
- With persistent indexing, only changed files are re-indexed; concurrent operations use async I/O, making large vaults (10,000+ notes) usable.

- RAG frameworks like LightRAG have seen significant updates in 2025, including support for RAGAS evaluation and Langfuse tracing, enhancing reliability and performance.

### Key Takeaways

Obsidian handles moderate vaults (up to ~5,000–10,000 notes) well on desktop. Beyond that, indexing time, graph view rendering, and link autocomplete degrade significantly. For very large vaults (50K+), mobile performance is particularly impacted. In 2025, external tools like `obsidian-mcp` (with SQLite-backed incremental indexing) and RAG integrations provide scalable alternatives for search and retrieval at scale.

Here's a comprehensive overview of **MCP Server Architecture, Modular Plugin Registry Patterns, and Scalable Tool Organization in 2025**:

---

## Core Architecture

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) follows a client-host-server architecture where each host can run multiple client instances. This architecture enables users to integrate AI capabilities across applications while maintaining clear security boundaries and isolating concerns.

The MCP architecture follows a modular client–server design that cleanly separates the Host Application, MCP Client, and MCP Server, ensuring predictable and scalable integrations. It enables standardized tool discovery and execution, allowing AI agents to interact with external systems through schemas instead of custom integrations.

Built on JSON-RPC, MCP provides a stateful session protocol focused on context exchange and sampling coordination between clients and servers. The protocol uses a capability-based negotiation system where clients and servers explicitly declare their supported features during initialization.

## Modular Plugin & Registry Pattern

### The MCP Registry

The MCP Registry offers a structured mechanism for AI applications and tool clients to discover and connect to MCP servers. First launched in preview in September 2025, the registry aims to reduce fragmentation in the MCP ecosystem by providing a shared metadata catalog of servers. It is designed to support extension and federation, so that organizations can build custom sub-registries while conforming to a consistent interface.

Before the registry existed, MCP clients and ecosystem actors maintained disparate catalogs, enterprises built ad hoc internal registries, and server authors lacked a standard publishing path. This led to duplicated effort, inconsistent metadata views, and discovery friction.

### Federation Model

One of the registry's key architectural decisions is to embrace federation: the upstream MCP Registry is not the only registry. Instead, it serves as the canonical source of public MCP server metadata that subregistries (public or private) can ingest, augment, or mirror.

- Public subregistries (e.g., marketplaces tied to specific clients) can enrich metadata with user ratings, audit info, and search filters.
- Private subregistries within enterprises can combine published servers with internal ones, apply custom policies, and share a consistent API surface with MCP clients.

The MCP Registry was launched as the central index for all available MCP servers and had close to two thousand entries by November 2025 — a 407% growth from the initial batch of servers onboarded in September.

## Scalable Tool Organization

### Modular Design Principles

Instead of relying on rigid integrations or single-purpose connectors, MCP uses modular protocols that allow developers to plug in new capabilities without overhauling the core system. By separating communication logic from business logic, the architecture improves maintainability and scalability. Each module handles a specific function such as authentication, data exchange, or command execution, allowing teams to scale or update components independently.

Enterprises adopt MCP architecture for its security isolation, interoperability, and ease of extensibility, allowing teams to add new tools without modifying the core AI application.

### MCP Gateway Pattern

Rather than accepting the complexity of multiple MCP servers as inevitable, there's a better architectural approach — an MCP Gateway. An MCP Gateway functions as a reverse proxy and orchestrator positioned between LLM clients and MCP servers. You can think of it as an intelligent traffic controller that routes requests and enhances them.

### Extensions System

The protocol introduces extensions — components and conventions that operate outside the core specification, providing a flexible way to build scenario-specific additions that follow MCP conventions without requiring full protocol integration. This approach allows for experimentation and specialized use cases while keeping the core protocol focused and stable.

Extensions are designed to be:
- **Optional**: Server and client implementors can choose to adopt these extensions.
- **Additive**: Extensions do not modify or break core protocol functionality; they add new capabilities while preserving core protocol behavior.
- **Composable**: Extensions are modular and designed to work together without conflicts, allowing implementations to adopt multiple extensions simultaneously.

### Tool Orchestration Patterns

The orchestration of tool calls is a central function of an MCP server. The planner tool pattern shifts the paradigm from reactive, step-by-step chaining to more proactive, plan-then-execute approaches. Two dominant patterns have emerged: Reactive Chaining (ReAct), where the LLM decides the next action after receiving previous results, with each step being a self-contained cycle of thought, action, and observation.

### Dynamic Registration & Auto-Discovery

ToolHive's Registry Server now auto-discovers server types and scales sync across multiple registry instances. It can automatically detect whether an auto-registered server is an MCPServer, VirtualMCPServer, or MCPRemoteProxy, scale sync jobs across multiple registry instances, and deploy without hardcoded namespaces by auto-discovering its operating namespace.

## Evolution & Roadmap

The MCP 2025-06-18 specification represents more than technical improvements — it signals that MCP is maturing from an experimental protocol into a production-ready foundation for AI-human collaboration.

The roadmap ahead includes deeper work on reliability and observability, making it easier to debug and monitor complex MCP deployments. The team is exploring better patterns for server composition, allowing you to build sophisticated capabilities by combining simpler building blocks, and continuing to refine the security model to meet the needs of the most demanding enterprise environments.

## Technical Research Scope Confirmation

**Research Topic:** Obsidian Vault & MCP Server Improvement for Cohezion
**Research Goals:** Leverage Obsidian capabilities to improve our vault and vault MCP server, with integration into PRD, Architecture, Epics, and Stories workflows

## Technology Stack Analysis

### Obsidian Core Platform

Obsidian is a local-first, Markdown-based knowledge management tool with an extensible plugin architecture. It stores all data as plain `.md` files on disk, making it fully interoperable with any tool that reads Markdown. As of 2025-2026, Obsidian has matured into a comprehensive PKM (Personal Knowledge Management) platform used at scale — one practitioner documented 8,000 notes with 64,000+ internal links managed over 3+ years.

_Core Architecture: Local-first markdown files, YAML frontmatter metadata, wiki-link graph, plugin extensibility_
_Current Version: 1.9+ with Properties system, Canvas, and Bases (database views)_
_Strengths: Zero vendor lock-in, offline-first, plain-text portability, massive plugin ecosystem_
_Source: [Obsidian Help](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [PKM at Scale](https://www.dsebastien.net/personal-knowledge-management-at-scale-analyzing-8-000-notes-and-64-000-links/)_

### Properties & Metadata System (YAML Frontmatter)

Obsidian supports 7 property types: **Text**, **List**, **Number**, **Checkbox**, **Date**, **Date & Time**, and **Tags**. Properties are stored as YAML frontmatter and enforced vault-wide — once a property name is assigned a type, ALL notes with that property must use the same type.

_Supported Types: text, list, number, checkbox, date, datetime, tags_
_Default Properties: `tags` (hierarchical), `aliases` (search), `cssclasses` (styling)_
_Limitation: No nested YAML support in visual editor (Source mode only for complex structures)_
_Vault-Wide Enforcement: Property type is consistent across entire vault_
_Source: [Obsidian Properties](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [DeepWiki Properties](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-help/4.3-properties-and-metadata)_

### Canvas System (JSON-Based Visual Workspace)

Canvas files (`.canvas`) use an open JSON format ([JSON Canvas spec](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)) with 4 node types: **file** (vault references), **text** (markdown), **link** (URLs), and **group** (containers). Edges connect nodes with directional arrows. Since canvas files are plain JSON, they can be programmatically generated, manipulated, and queried.

_Node Types: file, text, link, group — each with x/y/width/height positioning_
_Edge System: fromNode/toNode with side anchoring (top/right/bottom/left) and labels_
_Color System: 6 palette presets or hex values_
_Programmatic Tools: canvas_lib.py, obsidian-node-canvas, Advanced Canvas plugin_
_Source: [Canvas Help](https://help.obsidian.md/plugins/canvas), [Canvas API DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/4.1-canvas-api), [JSON Canvas GitHub](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)_

### Dataview Plugin (Query Engine)

Dataview treats an Obsidian vault as a queryable database. It indexes YAML frontmatter and inline fields (`[key:: value]`) and provides both a DQL query language and a JavaScript API (DataviewJS). It now uses IndexedDB caching for near-instant startup on repeat visits.

_Query Modes: DQL (table/list/task/calendar) and DataviewJS (full JavaScript)_
_Data Sources: YAML frontmatter, inline fields `[key:: value]`, tags, tasks_
_Caching: IndexedDB for fast startup on large vaults_
_Limitation: Read-only by design — cannot modify notes, only display/query_
_Source: [Dataview GitHub](https://github.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview), [Dataview Docs](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/), [Dataview API](https://deepwiki.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview/4-api-reference)_

### Templater Plugin (Template Automation)

Templater (3.8M+ downloads, 4,616 GitHub stars) provides dynamic template insertion with JavaScript execution. It supports conditional logic, file manipulation, system commands, and user prompt inputs. Combined with Dataview, it transforms Obsidian into an automation platform.

_Template Syntax: `<% %>` (variable expansion), `<%* %>` (JavaScript execution)_
_Capabilities: File creation, folder manipulation, date math, system commands, user prompts_
_Automation: Auto-apply templates on note creation, folder-based template matching_
_Source: [Templater GitHub](https://github.com/SilentVoid13/Templater), [Templater Scripts](https://github.com/mihaiconstantin/obsidian-templater-scripts)_

### Obsidian MCP Server Ecosystem (6+ Projects)

The MCP ecosystem for Obsidian has exploded in 2025-2026 with at least 24 MCP servers listed on mcp.so. Key implementations:

| Server | Approach | Key Differentiator |
|--------|----------|--------------------|
| [cyanheads/obsidian-mcp-server](https://github.com/cyanheads/obsidian-mcp-server) | REST API bridge | Comprehensive CRUD + frontmatter + tags |
| [bitbonsai/mcp-obsidian](https://github.com/bitbonsai/mcp-obsidian) | Universal AI bridge | Multi-client (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) + YAML safety |
| [aaronsb/obsidian-mcp-plugin](https://github.com/aaronsb/obsidian-mcp-plugin) | Graph-first | Semantic navigation + knowledge graph traversal |
| [jacksteamdev/obsidian-mcp-tools](https://github.com/jacksteamdev/obsidian-mcp-tools) | Semantic search | Vector search + Templater integration |
| [fiddeb/obsidian-mcp-server](https://lobehub.com/mcp/fiddeb-obsidian-mcp-server) | Go-based | Lightweight, VS Code integration |

_Ecosystem Size: 24+ MCP servers for Obsidian on mcp.so_
_Common Pattern: Obsidian Local REST API plugin as backend bridge_
_Source: [Obsidian Forum Discussion](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/obsidian-mcp-servers-experiences-and-recommendations/99936)_

### Cohezion Vault MCP Server (Current State)

Our existing server (`cloud-vault-mcp/`) implements **47 tools** across 12 categories in ~10,475 lines of Python. It runs as a FastMCP HTTP server on port 8360.

| Category | Tools | Purpose |
|----------|-------|---------|
| Core Vault Ops | 5 | Read/write/edit/delete/list notes |
| Obsidian-Aware | 4 | Backlinks, forward links, tags, templates |
| Full-Text Search | 1 | Regex search with folder scoping |
| Compound Engineering | 5 | Decisions, experiments, patterns, context search |
| Teleport Protocol | 5 | Cross-session task delegation |
| Session Context | 3 | State push/pull, memory bridge |
| Google Sheets | 6 | Research spreadsheet bridge |
| SurrealDB Graph | 5 | Graph sync, watchers, queries |
| Ollama Integration | 3 | Local LLM queries + embeddings |
| Agent Context | 3 | Session tracking, decision/outcome lineage |
| Text-to-Speech | 1 | Pocket TTS |
| Health Check | 1 | Full dependency health check |

_Templates: 6 types (decisions, experiments, patterns, papers, daily, projects)_
_Frontmatter: Standard YAML with date, tags, status, project fields_
_Security: Path validation, traversal prevention, optional TLS + API key auth_
_**GAP: No BMAD workflow integration (PRD, Architecture, Epics, Stories)**_

### Technology Adoption Trends

_MCP as Standard: Anthropic's MCP protocol has become the de facto AI-tool integration standard, with 24+ Obsidian implementations alone_
_Graph-First Knowledge: The trend is moving from flat file search toward semantic graph navigation (aaronsb's approach)_
_AI-Native Workflows: Users report 8-12 hours/week saved via AI-assisted Obsidian documentation workflows_
_Schema.org Integration: Emerging pattern of YAML-LD frontmatter for linked data compatibility_
_Source: [Obsidian AI Review](https://tutorialswithai.com/tools/obsidian-ai/), [Full Stack CX Workflow](https://www.fullstack.cx/blog/obsidian-documentation-workflow), [Schema.org Forum](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/schema-org-in-obsidian-using-yaml-ld-frontmatter-for-linked-data/109969)_

## Integration Patterns Analysis

### MCP Protocol Design Patterns (Current Best Practices)

MCP has been donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as of December 2025, with 97M+ monthly SDK downloads and backing from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft. The protocol defines three core primitives:

1. **Tools** — Functions that perform side effects (CRUD operations, calculations, API calls)
2. **Resources** — Read-only data endpoints that expose context to LLMs (files, database records, live data)
3. **Prompts** — Reusable prompt templates that clients can surface to users

**Key Finding:** Our vault MCP server currently only uses **Tools**. We are not leveraging **Resources** or **Prompts** at all. This is a significant gap — Resources would allow Claude to browse vault structure without tool calls, and Prompts would provide pre-built workflows for common BMAD operations.

_Design Principle: Focused single-purpose servers over monolithic mega-servers_
_Protocol Update (June 2025): Streamable HTTP replaces SSE, structured tool outputs, OAuth auth, elicitation_
_Tool Description Quality: Research shows 89.8% of MCP tools have "Unstated Limitations" and 84.3% have "Opaque Parameters" — tool descriptions need careful attention_
_Source: [MCP Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/best-practices/), [MCP Spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25), [Tool Description Smells](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.14878v1)_

### BMAD Artifact-to-Vault Integration Gap

The current Cohezion vault MCP server was designed for **knowledge persistence** (decisions, patterns, experiments) but has no integration with **BMAD workflow artifacts**. BMAD workflows produce structured documents with specific frontmatter:

| BMAD Artifact | Current Frontmatter | Storage | Vault Integration |
|---------------|---------------------|---------|-------------------|
| PRD | `workflowType: prd`, `stepsCompleted`, `inputDocuments` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Architecture | `workflowType: architecture`, `project_name`, `date` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Epics & Stories | `stepsCompleted`, `inputDocuments` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Research | `workflowType: research`, `research_type`, `research_topic` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/research/` | **None** |
| Implementation | Various | `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/` | **None** |

**The gap:** BMAD artifacts live in `_bmad-output/` and the vault lives in `cloud-vault-mcp/vault/`. These two systems don't talk to each other. Decisions made during BMAD workflows are not captured as vault ADRs. Stories completed don't generate patterns. Research doesn't feed into the knowledge graph.

### Proposed Integration Pattern: Bidirectional Bridge

The integration should work in both directions:

**BMAD → Vault (Forward Flow):**
- When a PRD is created/approved → Generate a `projects/` vault note with requirements summary
- When an Architecture Decision is made → Auto-create `decisions/` ADR in vault
- When an Epic is completed → Extract patterns to `patterns/` in vault
- When a Story is implemented → Log experiment/outcome in vault

**Vault → BMAD (Reverse Flow):**
- When creating a new PRD → Query vault for related decisions, patterns, and past experiments
- When planning architecture → Surface relevant ADRs and known anti-patterns from vault
- When writing stories → Pull implementation patterns and lessons learned from vault
- When running retrospectives → Aggregate vault decisions/experiments for the epic timeframe

_Pattern: Event-driven document lifecycle with frontmatter state tracking_
_ADR Standard: MADR (Markdown ADR) format with Proposed/Accepted/Rejected/Superseded states_
_Source: [MADR GitHub](https://github.com/adr/madr), [ADR Examples](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record)_

### MCP Resources for Vault Browsing

Instead of requiring tool calls to discover vault contents, MCP **Resources** can expose vault structure as browsable context:

```
vault://decisions/              → List all ADRs
vault://patterns/               → List all reusable patterns
vault://projects/{project}/     → All notes for a specific project
vault://bmad/prd/               → All PRDs (bridged from _bmad-output)
vault://bmad/epics/             → All epic breakdowns
vault://bmad/architecture/      → All architecture decisions
```

This follows the [MCP Resources specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/resources/) and allows the LLM to pull context without consuming tool-call quota.

### MCP Prompts for BMAD Workflows

MCP **Prompts** can standardize common BMAD-vault interactions:

| Prompt | Purpose | Arguments |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `create-prd-with-context` | Start PRD creation with vault knowledge pre-loaded | `project_name` |
| `architecture-decision` | Log architecture decision to both BMAD and vault | `title`, `context` |
| `epic-retrospective` | Generate retrospective from vault data for an epic | `epic_id` |
| `story-implementation-context` | Pull all relevant vault context for implementing a story | `story_id` |
| `research-synthesis` | Synthesize research notes into patterns | `research_topic` |

_Source: [MCP Prompts Documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/prompts/)_

### Canvas as Visual Workflow Board

Obsidian Canvas (`.canvas` JSON format) can be programmatically generated to create visual boards:

**Epic Board Canvas:** Auto-generate a canvas with:
- Group nodes per epic (color-coded by status)
- File nodes linking to each story `.md` file
- Edges showing story dependencies
- Text nodes for blockers and risks

**Architecture Decision Map Canvas:** Auto-generate:
- File nodes for each ADR in the vault
- Edges showing supersession chains (ADR-001 → ADR-005)
- Group nodes per domain (security, performance, data)
- Color coding by status (Accepted=green, Superseded=grey, Proposed=yellow)

_Source: [JSON Canvas Spec](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas), [Canvas API](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/4.1-canvas-api)_

### Frontmatter Standardization Strategy

To enable cross-system queries (Dataview in Obsidian, vault_search via MCP, SurrealDB graph), all BMAD and vault notes should share a standardized frontmatter schema:

```yaml
---
# Universal fields (all note types)
date: 2026-03-03           # ISO 8601
tags: [project/cohezion, type/prd]  # Hierarchical tags
status: active              # active | completed | superseded | archived
project: cohezion           # Project identifier
artifact_type: prd          # prd | architecture | epic | story | decision | pattern | experiment

# BMAD-specific fields
bmad_workflow: create-prd   # Which BMAD workflow created this
steps_completed: [1, 2, 3]  # Workflow progress
linked_artifacts:           # Cross-references
  - "[[decisions/2026-03-03-auth-strategy]]"
  - "[[patterns/jwt-token-pattern]]"

# Vault-specific fields

domain: security            # Domain classification
---
```

Two production MCP servers demonstrate best practices for document management with frontmatter:

1. **mcp-markdown-manager** (joelmnz) — Full-stack TypeScript system for AI agents to manage markdown articles with frontmatter. Provides Web UI + REST API + MCP server. Auto-generates metadata when frontmatter is missing.

2. **mcp-docs-service** (alekspetrov) — Markdown document service with CRUD operations, line-based editing, diff previews, and YAML frontmatter support. Returns minimum health score of 80 even with issues — resilient by design.

### Security Patterns for Vault Integration

Current vault MCP server security features (path validation, traversal prevention, optional TLS + API key) are solid. For BMAD integration, additional considerations:

## Architectural Patterns and Design

### System Architecture: Proposed Vault-BMAD Unified Architecture

The recommended architecture follows a **layered bridge pattern** that keeps the vault MCP server and BMAD workflows as separate concerns, connected by a bidirectional sync layer:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    MCP Clients                       │
│     (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, etc.)         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Vault MCP Server (FastMCP)              │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐      │
│  │ Tools    │ Resources│ Prompts  │ Canvas   │      │
│  │ (CRUD)   │ (Browse) │ (Workflows)│(Visual)│      │
│  └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              BMAD Bridge Layer (NEW)                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │ Artifact Sync │ State Machine │ Frontmatter│      │
│  │ Engine        │ Lifecycle     │ Normalizer │      │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
├──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┤
│  Vault Storage       │  BMAD Output                  │
│  cloud-vault-mcp/    │  _bmad-output/                │
│  vault/              │  planning-artifacts/           │
│  ├── decisions/      │  ├── PRDs                     │
│  ├── patterns/       │  ├── architecture/            │
│  ├── experiments/    │  ├── research/                │
│  ├── projects/       │  implementation-artifacts/     │
│  ├── bmad/  (NEW)    │  ├── stories/                 │
│  └── canvas/ (NEW)   │  └── retrospectives/          │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
```

This architecture follows the MCP best practice of **focused, single-purpose modules** rather than a monolithic server. The BMAD Bridge Layer is a new module within the existing server, not a separate server.

_Design Principle: Separation of concerns — vault stores knowledge, BMAD stores workflow artifacts, bridge synchronizes between them_
_Pattern: Adapter/Bridge pattern with event-driven sync_
_Source: [MCP Architecture](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/architecture), [MCP Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/best-practices/)_

### Document Lifecycle State Machine

Inspired by Veeva Vault's document lifecycle system, BMAD artifacts should follow a state machine pattern with well-defined transitions:

```
PRD Lifecycle:        Draft → In Review → Approved → Archived
                              ↓
                          Needs Revision ←──┘

Architecture:         Proposed → Accepted → Superseded
                         ↓
                      Rejected

Epic Lifecycle:       Defined → In Progress → Completed → Retrospected
                                    ↓
                               Blocked → Unblocked → In Progress

Story Lifecycle:      Draft → Ready → In Progress → Done → Verified
                                          ↓
                                       Blocked
```

Each state transition triggers vault actions:
- **PRD Approved** → Generate `projects/` vault note with requirements summary
- **Architecture Accepted** → Create `decisions/` ADR in vault
- **Epic Completed** → Extract `patterns/` from implementation
- **Story Verified** → Log `experiments/` outcome

_Pattern: State machine with event-driven side effects_
_Reference: [Veeva Vault Lifecycles](https://platform.veevavault.help/en/lr/2434/), [MADR Status Values](https://github.com/adr/madr)_

### MCP Server Modular Extension Pattern

The MCP ecosystem has matured to support modular extension patterns. Our server should adopt:

**1. Capability-Based Registration:**
```python
# Each module declares its capabilities at init
class BMADBridge:
    capabilities = {
        "tools": ["bmad_sync_prd", "bmad_create_epic_board", ...],
        "resources": ["vault://bmad/prd/*", "vault://bmad/epics/*"],
        "prompts": ["create-prd-with-context", "epic-retrospective"]
    }
```

**2. MCP Gateway Pattern** for complex operations:
Instead of one mega-tool that does everything, compose smaller tools:
- `vault_read` → reads any note
- `bmad_enrich` → adds vault context to a BMAD artifact
- `bmad_sync` → pushes BMAD artifact changes to vault

**3. Extensions System** (from MCP spec):
BMAD integration can be built as an MCP extension — optional, additive, and composable. This means users who don't use BMAD can still use the vault server without the bridge.

_MCP Registry: ~2,000 entries by November 2025, 407% growth in 3 months_
_Pattern: Federation model — canonical registry + private sub-registries_
_Source: [MCP Registry Architecture](https://workos.com/blog/mcp-registry-architecture-technical-overview), [MCP Gateway](https://www.infracloud.io/blogs/mcp-gateway/), [MCP Extensions](http://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025-11-25-first-mcp-anniversary/)_

### Scalability and Performance Patterns

**Vault Scale Considerations:**
- Obsidian handles 5,000-10,000 notes well on desktop
- Beyond 50K notes, indexing and graph view degrade significantly (130K-note vault takes ~10 min to index)
- Our vault currently has <200 notes — well within comfortable limits
- With BMAD integration adding ~50-100 artifacts per project, we stay under 1,000 notes for years

**Search Performance Architecture:**
Our current regex-based search is adequate for current scale. For future growth:

| Scale | Strategy | Implementation |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| <1,000 notes | Regex full-text (current) | `vault_search()` with SearchCache TTL |
| 1,000-5,000 | SQLite FTS5 index | Like `obsidian-mcp` PyPI package — 5x faster, 90% less memory |
| 5,000+ | Vector embeddings + HNSW | Leverage existing Ollama `ollama_embed()` + Qdrant/Milvus |
| Graph queries | SurrealDB (existing) | Already have `surrealdb_query()` for relationship traversal |

**Incremental Indexing** (key insight from `obsidian-mcp` PyPI):
Only re-index changed files rather than full vault scan. Use file modification timestamps + hash comparison.

_Desktop Scale: 5K-10K notes comfortable, 50K+ degrades_
_SQLite FTS5: 5x search speedup over regex, 90% memory reduction_
_Source: [Obsidian Scale Discussion](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/terabyte-size-million-notes-vaults-how-scalable-is-obsidian/66674), [obsidian-mcp PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/obsidian-mcp/), [RAG Integration](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rag-personal-knowledge-management-obsidian-integration/)_

### Canvas Generation Architecture

For programmatic canvas generation (epic boards, ADR maps, architecture diagrams), the architecture should:

1. **Query vault for artifacts** → Get all epics/stories/ADRs with frontmatter metadata
2. **Layout engine** → Calculate node positions using a grid or force-directed layout
3. **Generate JSON** → Produce valid `CanvasData` with nodes, edges, groups
4. **Write to vault** → Save as `.canvas` file, viewable in Obsidian

```python
class CanvasGenerator:
    def generate_epic_board(self, project: str) -> CanvasData:
        epics = self.query_artifacts(project, type="epic")
        nodes, edges = [], []
        for i, epic in enumerate(epics):
            group = GroupNode(id=epic.id, label=epic.title, x=0, y=i*300, width=800, height=250)
            nodes.append(group)
            for j, story in enumerate(epic.stories):
                node = FileNode(id=story.id, file=story.path, x=50+j*200, y=i*300+50)
                nodes.append(node)
                edges.append(Edge(from_node=group.id, to_node=node.id))
        return CanvasData(nodes=nodes, edges=edges)
```

_Canvas Format: JSON with nodes[] and edges[], fully programmable_
_Layout Options: Grid (simple), force-directed (complex relationships)_

### Data Architecture: Unified Frontmatter Schema

The key architectural decision is a **unified frontmatter schema** that works across both vault notes and BMAD artifacts:

**Tier 1 (Universal — all notes):**
```yaml
date: 2026-03-03
tags: [project/cohezion]
status: active
project: cohezion
```

**Tier 2 (Artifact-typed — BMAD bridge notes):**
```yaml
artifact_type: prd | architecture | epic | story | decision | pattern | experiment
bmad_source: _bmad-output/planning-artifacts/prd-cohezion.md  # Source file path
linked_artifacts:
  - "[[decisions/2026-03-03-auth-strategy]]"
```

**Tier 3 (Type-specific — varies by artifact):**
```yaml
# For PRDs:
stakeholders: [Mike]
priority: high

# For Epics:
stories_total: 8
stories_done: 5
sprint: sprint-3

# For Decisions:
decision_status: accepted  # proposed | accepted | rejected | superseded
superseded_by: "[[decisions/2026-04-01-new-approach]]"
```

This tiered approach respects Obsidian's property type enforcement (same property = same type vault-wide) while providing rich queryable metadata.

_Constraint: Obsidian enforces single type per property name across entire vault_
_Pattern: Tiered schema — universal + typed + specific layers_

### Security Architecture

The existing vault MCP server security model is sound (path validation, traversal prevention, TLS, API key auth). For BMAD integration, add:

1. **Artifact provenance**: Every vault note synced from BMAD includes `bmad_source` in frontmatter for audit trail
2. **Sync conflict resolution**: Last-write-wins with conflict detection (hash comparison) and user notification
3. **Scope isolation**: BMAD bridge tools operate within designated folders (`vault/bmad/`) only
4. **Read-only resources**: MCP Resources are inherently read-only — safe for browsing BMAD artifacts without write risk

_Security Model: Defense in depth — path validation + folder scoping + provenance tracking_
_Source: [MCP Security Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/best-practices/), [Zeo MCP Security](https://zeo.org/resources/blog/mcp-server-architecture-state-management-security-tool-orchestration)_

## Technology Stack Analysis

### Obsidian Core Platform

Obsidian is a local-first, Markdown-based knowledge management tool with an extensible plugin architecture. It stores all data as plain `.md` files on disk, making it fully interoperable with any tool that reads Markdown. As of 2025-2026, Obsidian has matured into a comprehensive PKM (Personal Knowledge Management) platform used at scale — one practitioner documented 8,000 notes with 64,000+ internal links managed over 3+ years.

_Core Architecture: Local-first markdown files, YAML frontmatter metadata, wiki-link graph, plugin extensibility_
_Current Version: 1.9+ with Properties system, Canvas, and Bases (database views)_
_Strengths: Zero vendor lock-in, offline-first, plain-text portability, massive plugin ecosystem_
_Source: [Obsidian Help](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [PKM at Scale](https://www.dsebastien.net/personal-knowledge-management-at-scale-analyzing-8-000-notes-and-64-000-links/)_

### Properties & Metadata System (YAML Frontmatter)

Obsidian supports 7 property types: **Text**, **List**, **Number**, **Checkbox**, **Date**, **Date & Time**, and **Tags**. Properties are stored as YAML frontmatter and enforced vault-wide — once a property name is assigned a type, ALL notes with that property must use the same type.

_Supported Types: text, list, number, checkbox, date, datetime, tags_
_Default Properties: `tags` (hierarchical), `aliases` (search), `cssclasses` (styling)_
_Limitation: No nested YAML support in visual editor (Source mode only for complex structures)_
_Vault-Wide Enforcement: Property type is consistent across entire vault_
_Source: [Obsidian Properties](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [DeepWiki Properties](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-help/4.3-properties-and-metadata)_

### Canvas System (JSON-Based Visual Workspace)

Canvas files (`.canvas`) use an open JSON format ([JSON Canvas spec](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)) with 4 node types: **file** (vault references), **text** (markdown), **link** (URLs), and **group** (containers). Edges connect nodes with directional arrows. Since canvas files are plain JSON, they can be programmatically generated, manipulated, and queried.

_Node Types: file, text, link, group — each with x/y/width/height positioning_
_Edge System: fromNode/toNode with side anchoring (top/right/bottom/left) and labels_
_Color System: 6 palette presets or hex values_
_Programmatic Tools: canvas_lib.py, obsidian-node-canvas, Advanced Canvas plugin_
_Source: [Canvas Help](https://help.obsidian.md/plugins/canvas), [Canvas API DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/4.1-canvas-api), [JSON Canvas GitHub](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas)_

### Dataview Plugin (Query Engine)

Dataview treats an Obsidian vault as a queryable database. It indexes YAML frontmatter and inline fields (`[key:: value]`) and provides both a DQL query language and a JavaScript API (DataviewJS). It now uses IndexedDB caching for near-instant startup on repeat visits.

_Query Modes: DQL (table/list/task/calendar) and DataviewJS (full JavaScript)_
_Data Sources: YAML frontmatter, inline fields `[key:: value]`, tags, tasks_
_Caching: IndexedDB for fast startup on large vaults_
_Limitation: Read-only by design — cannot modify notes, only display/query_
_Source: [Dataview GitHub](https://github.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview), [Dataview Docs](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/), [Dataview API](https://deepwiki.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview/4-api-reference)_

### Templater Plugin (Template Automation)

Templater (3.8M+ downloads, 4,616 GitHub stars) provides dynamic template insertion with JavaScript execution. It supports conditional logic, file manipulation, system commands, and user prompt inputs. Combined with Dataview, it transforms Obsidian into an automation platform.

_Template Syntax: `<% %>` (variable expansion), `<%* %>` (JavaScript execution)_
_Capabilities: File creation, folder manipulation, date math, system commands, user prompts_
_Automation: Auto-apply templates on note creation, folder-based template matching_
_Source: [Templater GitHub](https://github.com/SilentVoid13/Templater), [Templater Scripts](https://github.com/mihaiconstantin/obsidian-templater-scripts)_

## Integration Patterns Analysis

### MCP Protocol Design Patterns (Current Best Practices)

MCP has been donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as of December 2025, with 97M+ monthly SDK downloads and backing from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft. The protocol defines three core primitives:

1. **Tools** — Functions that perform side effects (CRUD operations, calculations, API calls)
2. **Resources** — Read-only data endpoints that expose context to LLMs (files, database records, live data)
3. **Prompts** — Reusable prompt templates that clients can surface to users

**Key Finding:** Our vault MCP server currently only uses **Tools**. We are not leveraging **Resources** or **Prompts** at all. This is a significant gap — Resources would allow Claude to browse vault structure without tool calls, and Prompts would provide pre-built workflows for common BMAD operations.

_Design Principle: Focused single-purpose servers over monolithic mega-servers_
_Protocol Update (June 2025): Streamable HTTP replaces SSE, structured tool outputs, OAuth auth, elicitation_
_Tool Description Quality: Research shows 89.8% of MCP tools have "Unstated Limitations" and 84.3% have "Opaque Parameters" — tool descriptions need careful attention_
_Source: [MCP Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/best-practices/), [MCP Spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25), [Tool Description Smells](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.14878v1)_

### BMAD Artifact-to-Vault Integration Gap

The current Cohezion vault MCP server was designed for **knowledge persistence** (decisions, patterns, experiments) but has no integration with **BMAD workflow artifacts**. BMAD workflows produce structured documents with specific frontmatter:

| BMAD Artifact | Current Frontmatter | Storage | Vault Integration |
|---------------|---------------------|---------|-------------------|
| PRD | `workflowType: prd`, `stepsCompleted`, `inputDocuments` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Architecture | `workflowType: architecture`, `project_name`, `date` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Epics & Stories | `stepsCompleted`, `inputDocuments` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/` | **None** |
| Research | `workflowType: research`, `research_type`, `research_topic` | `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/research/` | **None** |
| Implementation | Various | `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/` | **None** |

**The gap:** BMAD artifacts live in `_bmad-output/` and the vault lives in `cloud-vault-mcp/vault/`. These two systems don't talk to each other. Decisions made during BMAD workflows are not captured as vault ADRs. Stories completed don't generate patterns. Research doesn't feed into the knowledge graph.

### Proposed Integration Pattern: Bidirectional Bridge

The integration should work in both directions:

**BMAD → Vault (Forward Flow):**
- When a PRD is created/approved → Generate a `projects/` vault note with requirements summary
- When an Architecture Decision is made → Auto-create `decisions/` ADR in vault
- When an Epic is completed → Extract patterns to `patterns/` in vault
- When a Story is implemented → Log experiment/outcome in vault

**Vault → BMAD (Reverse Flow):**
- When creating a new PRD → Query vault for related decisions, patterns, and past experiments
- When planning architecture → Surface relevant ADRs and known anti-patterns from vault
- When writing stories → Pull implementation patterns and lessons learned from vault
- When running retrospectives → Aggregate vault decisions/experiments for the epic timeframe

_Pattern: Event-driven document lifecycle with frontmatter state tracking_
_ADR Standard: MADR (Markdown ADR) format with Proposed/Accepted/Rejected/Superseded states_
_Source: [MADR GitHub](https://github.com/adr/madr), [ADR Examples](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record)_

### MCP Resources for Vault Browsing

Instead of requiring tool calls to discover vault contents, MCP **Resources** can expose vault structure as browsable context:

```
vault://decisions/              → List all ADRs
vault://patterns/               → List all reusable patterns
vault://projects/{project}/     → All notes for a specific project
vault://bmad/prd/               → All PRDs (bridged from _bmad-output)
vault://bmad/epics/             → All epic breakdowns
vault://bmad/architecture/      → All architecture decisions
```

This follows the [MCP Resources specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/resources/) and allows the LLM to pull context without consuming tool-call quota.

### MCP Prompts for BMAD Workflows

MCP **Prompts** can standardize common BMAD-vault interactions:

| Prompt | Purpose | Arguments |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `create-prd-with-context` | Start PRD creation with vault knowledge pre-loaded | `project_name` |
| `architecture-decision` | Log architecture decision to both BMAD and vault | `title`, `context` |
| `epic-retrospective` | Generate retrospective from vault data for an epic | `epic_id` |
| `story-implementation-context` | Pull all relevant vault context for implementing a story | `story_id` |
| `research-synthesis` | Synthesize research notes into patterns | `research_topic` |

_Source: [MCP Prompts Documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/prompts/)_

### Canvas as Visual Workflow Board

Obsidian Canvas (`.canvas` JSON format) can be programmatically generated to create visual boards:

**Epic Board Canvas:** Auto-generate a canvas with:
- Group nodes per epic (color-coded by status)
- File nodes linking to each story `.md` file
- Edges showing story dependencies
- Text nodes for blockers and risks

**Architecture Decision Map Canvas:** Auto-generate:
- File nodes for each ADR in the vault
- Edges showing supersession chains (ADR-001 → ADR-005)
- Group nodes per domain (security, performance, data)
- Color coding by status (Accepted=green, Superseded=grey, Proposed=yellow)

_Canvas Schema: CanvasData with nodes[] and edges[] — fully programmable via JSON_
_Source: [JSON Canvas Spec](https://github.com/obsidianmd/jsoncanvas), [Canvas API](https://deepwiki.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/4.1-canvas-api)_

### Frontmatter Standardization Strategy

To enable cross-system queries (Dataview in Obsidian, vault_search via MCP, SurrealDB graph), all BMAD and vault notes should share a standardized frontmatter schema:

```yaml
---
# Universal fields (all note types)
date: 2026-03-03           # ISO 8601
tags: [project/cohezion, type/prd]  # Hierarchical tags
status: active              # active | completed | superseded | archived
project: cohezion           # Project identifier
artifact_type: prd          # prd | architecture | epic | story | decision | pattern | experiment

# BMAD-specific fields
bmad_workflow: create-prd   # Which BMAD workflow created this
steps_completed: [1, 2, 3]  # Workflow progress
linked_artifacts:           # Cross-references
  - "[[decisions/2026-03-03-auth-strategy]]"
  - "[[patterns/jwt-token-pattern]]"

# Vault-specific fields
confidence: high            # high | medium | low
domain: security            # Domain classification
---
```

_Property Type Consistency: Obsidian enforces same type for same property name across entire vault_
_Limitation: No nested YAML in Obsidian visual editor_
_Source: [Obsidian Properties](https://help.obsidian.md/properties), [Frontmatter Generator Plugin](https://www.obsidianstats.com/plugins/frontmatter-generator)_

### Document CRUD MCP Patterns (Industry Reference)

Two production MCP servers demonstrate best practices for document management with frontmatter:

1. **mcp-markdown-manager** (joelmnz) — Full-stack TypeScript system for AI agents to manage markdown articles with frontmatter. Provides Web UI + REST API + MCP server. Auto-generates metadata when frontmatter is missing.

2. **mcp-docs-service** (alekspetrov) — Markdown document service with CRUD operations, line-based editing, diff previews, and YAML frontmatter support. Returns minimum health score of 80 even with issues — resilient by design.

_Key Insight: Both servers treat frontmatter as first-class queryable metadata, not just passthrough text_
_Source: [Article Manager](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/@joelmnz/mcp-markdown-manager), [MCP Docs Service](https://mcpservers.org/servers/alekspetrov/mcp-docs-service)_

### Security Patterns for Vault Integration

Current vault MCP server security features (path validation, traversal prevention, optional TLS + API key) are solid. For BMAD integration, additional considerations:

- **Scope isolation**: BMAD artifacts may contain proprietary product requirements — ensure vault access is project-scoped
- **Human-in-the-loop**: MCP spec mandates explicit user consent before tool invocation — maintain for write operations
- **Audit trail**: Log all BMAD→vault syncs for traceability (who created which ADR from which PRD section)

_MCP Security Guidance: "Implementors SHOULD build robust consent and authorization flows"_
_Source: [MCP Architecture](https://modelcontextprotocol.info/docs/concepts/architecture/), [MCP Enterprise Guide](https://guptadeepak.com/the-complete-guide-to-model-context-protocol-mcp-enterprise-adoption-market-trends-and-implementation-strategies/)_

+### System Architecture: Proposed Vault-BMAD Unified Architecture
+The recommended architecture follows a **layered bridge pattern** that keeps the vault MCP server and BMAD workflows as separate concerns, connected by a bidirectional sync layer:

+This architecture follows the MCP best practice of **focused, single-purpose modules** rather than a monolithic server. The BMAD Bridge Layer is a new module within the existing server, not a separate server.
+_Design Principle: Separation of concerns — vault stores knowledge, BMAD stores workflow artifacts, bridge synchronizes between them_
+Inspired by Veeva Vault's document lifecycle system, BMAD artifacts should follow a state machine pattern with well-defined transitions:
+PRD Lifecycle:        Draft → In Review → Approved → Archived
+Epic Lifecycle:       Defined → In Progress → Completed → Retrospected
+Story Lifecycle:      Draft → Ready → In Progress → Done → Verified
+- **PRD Approved** → Generate `projects/` vault note with requirements summary
+_Pattern: State machine with event-driven side effects_
+The MCP ecosystem has matured to support modular extension patterns. Our server should adopt:
+# Each module declares its capabilities at init
+**2. MCP Gateway Pattern** for complex operations:
+Instead of one mega-tool that does everything, compose smaller tools:
+- `bmad_enrich` → adds vault context to a BMAD artifact
+- `bmad_sync` → pushes BMAD artifact changes to vault
+BMAD integration can be built as an MCP extension — optional, additive, and composable. This means users who don't use BMAD can still use the vault server without the bridge.
+_MCP Registry: ~2,000 entries by November 2025, 407% growth in 3 months_
+_Pattern: Federation model — canonical registry + private sub-registries_
+- Obsidian handles 5,000-10,000 notes well on desktop
+- Beyond 50K notes, indexing and graph view degrade significantly (130K-note vault takes ~10 min to index)
+- Our vault currently has <200 notes — well within comfortable limits
+- With BMAD integration adding ~50-100 artifacts per project, we stay under 1,000 notes for years
+Our current regex-based search is adequate for current scale. For future growth:
+| <1,000 notes | Regex full-text (current) | `vault_search()` with SearchCache TTL |
+| 1,000-5,000 | SQLite FTS5 index | Like `obsidian-mcp` PyPI package — 5x faster, 90% less memory |
+| 5,000+ | Vector embeddings + HNSW | Leverage existing Ollama `ollama_embed()` + Qdrant/Milvus |
+| Graph queries | SurrealDB (existing) | Already have `surrealdb_query()` for relationship traversal |
+Only re-index changed files rather than full vault scan. Use file modification timestamps + hash comparison.
+_SQLite FTS5: 5x search speedup over regex, 90% memory reduction_
+For programmatic canvas generation (epic boards, ADR maps, architecture diagrams), the architecture should:
+1. **Query vault for artifacts** → Get all epics/stories/ADRs with frontmatter metadata
+2. **Layout engine** → Calculate node positions using a grid or force-directed layout
+3. **Generate JSON** → Produce valid `CanvasData` with nodes, edges, groups
+4. **Write to vault** → Save as `.canvas` file, viewable in Obsidian
+            group = GroupNode(id=epic.id, label=epic.title, x=0, y=i*300, width=800, height=250)
+_Canvas Format: JSON with nodes[] and edges[], fully programmable_
+The key architectural decision is a **unified frontmatter schema** that works across both vault notes and BMAD artifacts:
+artifact_type: prd | architecture | epic | story | decision | pattern | experiment
+This tiered approach respects Obsidian's property type enforcement (same property = same type vault-wide) while providing rich queryable metadata.
+_Constraint: Obsidian enforces single type per property name across entire vault_
+_Pattern: Tiered schema — universal + typed + specific layers_
+The existing vault MCP server security model is sound (path validation, traversal prevention, TLS, API key auth). For BMAD integration, add:
+1. **Artifact provenance**: Every vault note synced from BMAD includes `bmad_source` in frontmatter for audit trail
+2. **Sync conflict resolution**: Last-write-wins with conflict detection (hash comparison) and user notification
+3. **Scope isolation**: BMAD bridge tools operate within designated folders (`vault/bmad/`) only
+4. **Read-only resources**: MCP Resources are inherently read-only — safe for browsing BMAD artifacts without write risk
+_Security Model: Defense in depth — path validation + folder scoping + provenance tracking_

Here's a comprehensive overview of building a FastMCP Python server with resources, prompts, and tools based on the latest guides and documentation:

## FastMCP Python Server: Resources & Prompts Implementation Guide

### Overview

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects LLMs to tools and data. FastMCP gives you everything you need to go from prototype to production. Today, the actively maintained standalone project is downloaded a million times a day, and some version of FastMCP powers 70% of MCP servers across all languages.

### Three Core Components

MCP provides three main primitives: **tools**, **resources**, and **prompts**. Tools are executable functions that perform actions or computations. Resources are data entities that your server exposes — these can be static or dynamic. Prompts are reusable templates that guide AI interactions, helping structure the way an AI model asks questions or explains concepts.

### Getting Started

Every FastMCP application starts with an instance of the `FastMCP` class. This object acts as the container for all your tools and resources.

### 1. Adding Tools

Tools are functions that an LLM can execute. To create a tool, simply write a standard Python function and decorate it with `@mcp.tool`. FastMCP automatically uses the function name as the tool's name and the function's docstring as the tool's description for the LLM.

### 2. Adding Resources

While tools enable actions, resources provide read-only access to data. Resources use URI patterns to create intuitive, REST-like interfaces for accessing information. They're ideal for exposing configuration, state, or any data that AI assistants might need to reference. The key difference: tools perform actions ("do something"), while resources retrieve information ("get something").

Resources can be **static** or **dynamic (templated)**:

- **Static resource**: Use `@mcp.resource("resource://config")` with a fixed URI.
- **Dynamic resource template**: Use a URI pattern like `@mcp.resource("greetings://{name}")` to generate personalized content based on parameters.

While you might expect FastMCP to use the function's docstring as the resource description, in practice, the docstring is not always picked up reliably. To ensure your resource has a clear, visible description, you should always provide the `description` argument explicitly in the decorator.

### 3. Adding Prompts

The `@mcp.prompt` decorator creates a reusable template. This isn't just a simple prompt; it's a strategic plan that instructs an LLM on how to use the server's tools in a sequence to perform a complex task.

For more complex prompts with multi-turn messages, the official MCP Python SDK shows how to use `base.UserMessage` and `base.AssistantMessage` for structured prompt flows.

### Complete Example

From the official FastMCP tutorial site (gofastmcp.com):

```python
from fastmcp import FastMCP

# 1. Create the server
mcp = FastMCP(name="My First MCP Server")

# 2. Add a tool
@mcp.tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Adds two integer numbers together."""
    return a + b

# 3. Add a static resource
@mcp.resource("resource://config")
def get_config() -> dict:
    """Provides the application's configuration."""
    return {"version": "1.0", "author": "MyTeam"}

# 4. Add a resource template for dynamic content
@mcp.resource("greetings://{name}")
def personalized_greeting(name: str) -> str:
    """Generates a personalized greeting."""
    return f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to the MCP server."

# 5. Run the server
if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
```

### Error Handling

FastMCP provides two main strategies: client-visible errors using `ToolError` for expected issues, and masked errors for internal failures. This dual approach ensures security while maintaining helpful error messages for AI assistants.

### Async Support

FastMCP automatically handles both sync and async functions. Use async for I/O-bound operations like database queries or API calls to improve server performance.

### Key Resources

| Resource | URL |
|----------|-----|
| **Official Docs** | [gofastmcp.com](https://gofastmcp.com/tutorials/create-mcp-server) |
| **GitHub Repo** | [github.com/jlowin/fastmcp](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) |
| **PyPI** | [pypi.org/project/fastmcp](https://pypi.org/project/fastmcp/) |
| **MCP Python SDK** | [github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk) |
| **Firecrawl Tutorial** | [firecrawl.dev/blog/fastmcp-tutorial](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/fastmcp-tutorial-building-mcp-servers-python) |
| **DataCamp Guide** | [datacamp.com](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/building-mcp-server-client-fastmcp) |

The latest version available on PyPI is fastmcp 3.1.0. When you're ready to deploy, Prefect Horizon offers free hosting for FastMCP users.

Here are the search results covering Obsidian vault MCP servers with markdown frontmatter support and pytest-based testing strategies:

---

## Key Projects Found

### 1. **markdown-frontmatter-mcp** (by caffeinatedwes)
A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that queries Markdown files by front matter metadata, designed for Obsidian vaults and other Markdown-based knowledge bases. Existing tools can search by keywords or do semantic search, but none let you query by front matter metadata — filtering by tags AND recency. It exposes a `query_recent_notes` tool that filters by tags, how far back to look (days), which folders to search, and max results. For testing, you can set your KB path and run the server directly for testing with `python3 src/server.py`.

### 2. **mcp-obsidian** (by bitbonsai)
A universal AI bridge for Obsidian vaults using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard, connecting any MCP-compatible AI assistant to your knowledge base. This server provides safe read/write access to your notes while preventing YAML frontmatter corruption. Security features include YAML Frontmatter Validation (parsed and validated before writing), Function/Symbol Prevention (dangerous JavaScript objects blocked from frontmatter), and Data Type Checking (only safe data types allowed).

### 3. **obsidian-mcp** (by punkpeye) — with pytest testing
Features include tag management (supporting both frontmatter and inline tags), link management, note insights, and AI-optimized error messages. This project has a comprehensive **pytest-based testing strategy**:
You can run all tests with `python tests/run_tests.py`, run specific test types including unit tests (requires pytest), integration tests (requires pytest), and live tests with real Obsidian, or run individual test files like `test_comprehensive.py` for full workflow tests and `test_data_validation.py` for data structure validation.

### 4. **obsidian-mcp-server** (by Vasallo94) — with pytest testing
This project also uses pytest extensively. Tests can be run with `uv run pytest`, with verbose output via `uv run pytest -v`, or for a specific test class like `uv run pytest tests/test_basic.py::TestConfiguration`. The test suite uses anyio for asynchronous tests. The project has a modular structure with tools organized by category (navigation, creation, analysis), resources, prompts, shared utilities, and includes `pytest.ini` for test configuration.

### 5. **markdown-editor-mcp-server** (by KazKozDev)
This is an MCP server providing tools for structured, semantic editing of Markdown files that understands the logical structure of documents, and is fully compliant with MCP 2025 Standard. Many Markdown tools (Obsidian, Jekyll) use YAML metadata at the top, and this tool allows the LLM to manage tags, dates, and properties without messing with the body text by updating or adding YAML Frontmatter to the document. Testing is straightforward: install for development with `pip install -e .` and run tests with `pytest tests/`.

### 6. **obsidian-mcp-server** (by cyanheads)
An Obsidian Knowledge-Management MCP server that enables AI agents and development tools to interact with an Obsidian vault, providing a comprehensive suite of tools for reading, writing, searching, and managing notes, tags, and frontmatter, acting as a bridge to the Obsidian Local REST API plugin. It atomically manages a note's YAML frontmatter with get, set, or delete operations on frontmatter keys. It features an intelligent in-memory vault cache service that improves performance, provides a fallback if the live API fails, and periodically refreshes to stay in sync.

---

## Summary of Testing Strategies

| Project | Testing Approach |
|---|---|
| **punkpeye/obsidian-mcp** | Unit, integration, and live tests via pytest; separate test files for workflows and data validation |
| **Vasallo94/obsidian-mcp-server** | pytest with anyio for async tests; `pytest.ini` config; specific test classes |
| **markdown-editor-mcp-server** | Simple `pytest tests/` execution |
| **markdown-frontmatter-mcp** | Manual server testing via direct execution |

The most mature pytest-based testing strategies are found in the **punkpeye/obsidian-mcp** and **Vasallo94/obsidian-mcp-server** projects, which separate tests into unit, integration, and live tiers.

Security features include YAML Frontmatter Validation (parsed and validated before writing), Function/Symbol Prevention (dangerous JavaScript objects blocked from frontmatter), and Data Type Checking (only safe data types allowed).

### 3. **obsidian-mcp** (by punkpeye) — with pytest testing
Features include tag management (supporting both frontmatter and inline tags), link management, note insights, and AI-optimized error messages. This project has a comprehensive **pytest-based testing strategy**:
You can run all tests with `python tests/run_tests.py`, run specific test types including unit tests (requires pytest), integration tests (requires pytest), and live tests with real Obsidian, or run individual test files like `test_comprehensive.py` for full workflow tests and `test_data_validation.py` for data structure validation.

### 4. **obsidian-mcp-server** (by Vasallo94) — with pytest testing
This project also uses pytest extensively. Tests can be run with `uv run pytest`, with verbose output via `uv run pytest -v`, or for a specific test class like `uv run pytest tests/test_basic.py::TestConfiguration`. The test suite uses anyio for asynchronous tests. The project has a modular structure with tools organized by category (navigation, creation, analysis), resources, prompts, shared utilities, and includes `pytest.ini` for test configuration.

### 5. **markdown-editor-mcp-server** (by KazKozDev)
This is an MCP server providing tools for structured, semantic editing of Markdown files that understands the logical structure of documents, and is fully compliant with MCP 2025 Standard. Many Markdown tools (Obsidian, Jekyll) use YAML metadata at the top, and this tool allows the LLM to manage tags, dates, and properties without messing with the body text by updating or adding YAML Frontmatter to the document. Testing is straightforward: install for development with `pip install -e .` and run tests with `pytest tests/`.

### 6. **obsidian-mcp-server** (by cyanheads)
An Obsidian Knowledge-Management MCP server that enables AI agents and development tools to interact with an Obsidian vault, providing a comprehensive suite of tools for reading, writing, searching, and managing notes, tags, and frontmatter, acting as a bridge to the Obsidian Local REST API plugin. It atomically manages a note's YAML frontmatter with get, set, or delete operations on frontmatter keys. It features an intelligent in-memory vault cache service that improves performance, provides a fallback if the live API fails, and periodically refreshes to stay in sync.

---

## Summary of Testing Strategies

| Project | Testing Approach |
|---|---|
| **punkpeye/obsidian-mcp** | Unit, integration, and live tests via pytest; separate test files for workflows and data validation |
| **Vasallo94/obsidian-mcp-server** | pytest with anyio for async tests; `pytest.ini` config; specific test classes |
| **markdown-editor-mcp-server** | Simple `pytest tests/` execution |
| **markdown-frontmatter-mcp** | Manual server testing via direct execution |

The most mature pytest-based testing strategies are found in the **punkpeye/obsidian-mcp** and **Vasallo94/obsidian-mcp-server** projects, which separate tests into unit, integration, and live tiers.
